Give me a month-by-month planting calendar for zone 7b.

Zone 7b in NC covers the central Piedmont — Greensboro, Winston-Salem, the northern Charlotte suburbs, and similar areas. Average last spring frost is around April 15; first fall frost runs October 25 to November 1. That gives you roughly a 193-day frost-free season, plus solid shoulder seasons on both ends.

JANUARY: Order seeds and plan bed layouts. Start onion seeds indoors around January 15–20 under lights — they need 10–12 weeks to size up before transplanting. Leeks too if you grow them.

FEBRUARY: Keep onion seedlings under lights, watering carefully. Mid-February, direct sow spinach, kale, and claytonia into garden beds — soil temps are cold but these crops germinate at 40°F. Row cover helps. Start perennial herbs (thyme, oregano, sage) from seed indoors.

MARCH: Start tomatoes, peppers, and eggplant under lights March 1–15, 6–8 weeks before last frost. Transplant onion seedlings outside after March 15 if soil is workable, spacing them 4–6 inches apart. Direct sow peas, lettuce, carrots, beets, radishes, and spinach outdoors. Plant potatoes mid-March: 2-oz seed pieces, 12 inches apart in rows 30 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep.

APRIL: Begin hardening off tomatoes and peppers in early April. Transplant brassica starts (broccoli, cabbage) started in February by April 1–15. After April 15, transplant tomatoes (18–24 inches apart), peppers (18 inches), and eggplant. Direct sow beans, cucumbers, squash, and corn after April 15. Plant corn in blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate pollination, plants 12 inches apart.

MAY: Succession sow beans every 2–3 weeks. Transplant basil after May 1 — it's genuinely cold-sensitive and struggles if nights drop below 50°F. Side-dress corn, squash, and tomatoes with compost or a balanced fertilizer when plants reach 12 inches. Plant sweet potato slips late May, 12 inches apart in raised ridges.

JUNE: Full summer garden underway. Watch closely for squash vine borers — they peak in June and July. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) to the crown of squash plants weekly starting when plants bloom, or use row cover until female flowers appear. First tomatoes typically ripen in late June for early varieties like Mountain Spring or Early Girl.

JULY: Harvest pressure is highest this month. Keep squash harvested every 2–3 days or production stops. Mid-July, start fall broccoli, cabbage, kale, and collard seeds indoors — these will be transplanted into the garden in August. Sow okra succession plantings.

AUGUST: Transplant fall brassica seedlings by August 1–15, spacing broccoli 18 inches apart, cabbage 18–24 inches, kale and collards 18 inches. Direct sow fall spinach, arugula, turnips, and mustard greens late August. As summer crops fade, pull them and amend beds with 2–3 inches of compost before planting fall crops.

SEPTEMBER: Your second-best growing season begins. Transplant any remaining fall brassica starts. Sow carrots (1/4 inch deep, thin to 3 inches) and beets (1 inch deep, thin to 4 inches) directly — they'll harvest November through December. Late September into mid-October is garlic planting time: cloves 2 inches deep, 6 inches apart, pointed end up. Oversow spinach for overwintering.

OCTOBER: Garlic goes in by mid-October. Plant cover crops in empty beds — winter rye at 2 lbs per 1,000 sq ft, or a mix of hairy vetch and winter rye at 1 lb each. Install row cover over tender fall crops when the first frost is forecast.

NOVEMBER: Harvest remaining fall crops before hard freezes. Carrots and parsnips left in ground get sweeter after frost — mulch them with 4–6 inches of straw and harvest through winter as needed. Collards and kale will survive most zone 7b winters with no protection.

DECEMBER: Clean and put away tools. Turn compost piles. Review the year's notes. Order any remaining seeds for next spring while selection is best.

How do I grow blueberries in NC? I heard the soil needs to be acidic.

You heard right — soil pH is the single most important factor, and getting it wrong is the most common reason blueberries fail in NC. They need a pH of 4.5–5.5. Most NC garden soils run 5.5–6.5 naturally, and soils that have been limed for vegetable gardens or lawns can be even higher. At pH 6 or above, blueberries can't take up iron and manganese properly, and they slowly yellow out and decline no matter how well you water and fertilize them.

Start with a soil test before you buy plants. The NCDA&CS soil lab in Raleigh charges $4 per sample and will tell you exactly what pH you're starting from. To lower pH, you use elemental sulfur — the rate depends on your current pH and soil type. As a rough guide, dropping pH by one unit in sandy loam takes about 1 lb of sulfur per 100 sq ft; in clay soil, closer to 1.5–2 lbs. Sulfur works slowly (bacteria have to convert it), so applying it 6–12 months before planting is ideal. If you're in a hurry, acidified planting mix (half pine bark fines, half native acidic soil) backfilled around each plant is a faster workaround for the planting hole.

For varieties, NC has two solid options. Rabbiteye blueberries (Tifblue, Climax, Brightwell, Premier) are heat- and drought-tolerant, do well across zones 7–8a, and grow to 6–8 feet at maturity. Southern Highbush types (O'Neal, Star, Reveille, Legacy) ripen 2–3 weeks earlier, stay smaller at 4–6 feet, and are a bit better for home gardens where you want manageable plants you can net easily. You need at least two different varieties for cross-pollination — one variety planted alone will produce almost nothing.

Planting basics: Rabbiteye 6 feet apart, Southern Highbush 4–5 feet apart, in rows 8–10 feet apart. Plant at the same depth the plant was in the container — don't plant deep. Immediately after planting, mulch 3–4 inches thick with pine bark, wood chips, or pine straw, keeping mulch 2 inches away from the crown. Blueberries have very shallow, fibrous roots with no root hairs — they can't compete with weeds and they dry out fast without mulch.

Water consistently the first two years, about 1–2 inches per week during the growing season. Go light on fertilizer the first year — a small application of cottonseed meal or an azalea-formulated fertilizer in early spring is enough. Heavy fertilizing burns young roots.

Expect modest production the first 2–3 years while plants establish. By year 4–5, a healthy plant will give you 5–10 lbs per season. The wait is worth it — established blueberries in well-maintained acid soil will produce for 30+ years.

What are the correct spacings for square foot gardening with cucumbers?

For square foot gardening, the standard recommendation is 1 plant per square foot — but that only works if you're growing vertically on a trellis. Without one, 1 per square foot is too crowded and you'll end up with a tangled, disease-prone mess.

If you're growing cucumbers on the ground, you need at least 2–3 square feet per plant. They'll produce, but airflow suffers, and in NC's summer humidity that's asking for trouble. Powdery mildew and angular leaf spot both thrive in the warm, still air under a dense canopy of sprawling cucumber vines.

The better approach for SFG in NC is to go vertical and commit to it. A 6-foot wooden stake, a cattle panel bent into an arch, or a simple string trellis all work. At 1 plant per square foot with vertical training, you get good airflow, easy harvesting, and you can see what you're doing when you're looking for cucumber beetles.

For variety selection in a square foot setup, bush types like Bush Pickle, Spacemaster, or Bush Champion are more manageable than open-pollinated vining types. They're less aggressive climbers and stay more compact. Vining types like Marketmore or Straight Eight will work, but they need consistent training or they'll sprawl off the trellis.

One thing worth knowing for NC specifically: cucumber plants here often burn out from disease and heat by late July or August. If you have 4–6 squares to work with, consider staggering plantings every 3 weeks starting late April through early June rather than planting all at once. That way you have productive plants coming on as older ones fade, and you stretch your harvest window from June into September.

I have a 4x12 raised bed. How should I lay it out using square foot gardening to grow the most food?

A 4x12 bed gives you 48 square feet to work with — that's genuinely productive space if you use it well. The core SFG rule is matching plants to their square footage: 1 per square for large plants like tomatoes, peppers, and broccoli; 4 per square for medium stuff like lettuce heads, basil, and chard; 9 per square for bush beans and spinach; 16 per square for small roots like radishes, carrots, and green onions.

For maximum output in NC, orient the long axis north-south if you can, and put your tallest plants at the north end so they don't shade everything else through the day.

Here's a layout that works well for our climate:

North end (4 squares): 2 indeterminate tomatoes — 'Cherokee Purple' and 'Mortgage Lifter' both perform reliably across the state — plus a 4-foot trellis section for pole beans or cucumbers (8–9 seeds per square going vertical). Vertical crops don't steal ground space.

Middle section (16 squares): 4 peppers (1 each), 4 Swiss chard (4 per square — it handles NC summer heat far better than spinach and you cut it repeatedly), 4 basil (4 per square — plant it near the tomatoes anyway), and 4 squares for broccoli or cauliflower in spring, which you can swap for fall transplants starting in August.

South end (28 squares — your fast-turnover zone): lettuce mix (4 per square), radishes (16 per square, harvested in 25–30 days), Danvers Half Long or Nantes carrots (16 per square — these varieties suit raised bed depth), and green onions (16 per square).

The thing most beginners don't fully use: in NC you get two full growing seasons. Spring transplants go out mid-February through April (later if you're in the mountains at 6b), and fall crops start again in late July through August. That south end fast-rotation zone can cycle 2–3 times a year, which is where you actually squeeze serious food production out of 48 square feet. Plan succession plantings rather than letting squares sit empty after a harvest.

Does mulching actually make a big difference in how often I need to water?

Yes — it's probably the single highest-return thing you can do besides installing drip irrigation. And in NC summers, it's not subtle.

Here's the basic mechanism: bare soil loses moisture through evaporation, especially when hot sun hits the surface directly. In a Piedmont or coastal plain July, an unprotected garden bed can dry out fast enough that daily watering becomes necessary. A 3-inch layer of organic mulch insulates the soil surface, blocks direct solar evaporation, and moderates soil temperature — which itself reduces plant water demand because stressed plants transpire more. NC State Extension data puts the irrigation reduction at 25–50% with proper mulching. In my experience, during peak summer heat it's closer to 50%.

For vegetable beds, shredded hardwood mulch or shredded leaves are excellent — 3 inches, kept about an inch away from plant stems to avoid crown rot. Pine straw is widely available across NC, cheap or free if you have pines, and it doesn't mat down and shed water the way whole leaves can. Also works great at 3–4 inches.

Fresh wood chips are fine for paths and permanent plantings but can temporarily tie up nitrogen in vegetable beds as they break down, so use aged chips if you go that route, or keep them out of the root zone.

One compounding benefit people overlook: mulch suppresses the weeds that would otherwise compete for that same soil moisture. So you're not just saving water directly — you're also eliminating a significant water draw from competitor plants. Top off whenever the layer compresses below 2 inches, which usually means once or twice a season.

I have a terrible fire ant problem in my garden beds. What's safe to use around food crops?

Fire ants are a real problem in NC garden beds — warm loose soil full of organic matter is exactly what they want. The good news is there are effective organic options that are genuinely safe around food crops.

The most effective approach is a two-step: bait the area broadly first, then treat individual mounds directly.

For broadcast treatment, spinosad-based fire ant bait — sold as Spinosad Fire Ant Bait or under the Ferti-lome label — is your best organic tool. Workers carry it back to the queen and it eventually knocks down the whole colony. It's slow (1–3 weeks to see full results), but it works. Apply at roughly 1–1.5 lbs per acre, which works out to about 1–2 tablespoons per 1,000 square feet broadcast, or about a tablespoon scattered 12–18 inches out from individual mounds where foragers are traveling — not on top of the mound. Apply in the evening when foragers are active and no rain is forecast for 24 hours. Spinosad bait degrades quickly when wet.

For mounds sitting directly in the bed where you want fast results, an orange oil drench works well: 1.5 oz of orange oil (d-limonene concentrate) plus 1 teaspoon dish soap per gallon of water. Pour 1–2 gallons directly into the mound center. It kills on contact by disrupting the ants' waxy cuticle and breaks down quickly in soil, leaving no meaningful residue. Boiling water (2–3 gallons per mound) also works but will damage any roots and soil life in that immediate area, which matters more in an active vegetable bed.

One realistic expectation: fire ants recolonize aggressively, especially in warm months. Even a successful knockdown can be followed by a new colony moving in within weeks. Consistent bait applications in spring (March–April) and fall (September–October) do more for long-term control than one-time treatments.
The spinosad bait — do I just broadcast it all over the garden beds or put it around individual mounds?

Both, ideally, but technique matters for each.

For broadcast treatment, sprinkle bait throughout the garden area and the surrounding 10–15 feet at the label rate — roughly 2.5 tablespoons per 1,000 square feet. This addresses colonies you haven't found yet and disrupts the broader local population, not just the mounds you can see. Don't water it in or rake it in — it needs to sit on the soil surface where foraging workers find it.

For visible mounds in the bed, scatter a tablespoon of bait in a ring about 12–18 inches out from the mound, not right on top. Foragers travel out from the mound to find food and carry it back; dropping bait at the entrance point misses a lot of the worker traffic.

Timing is critical and most people get this wrong. Apply when soil temperature is between 65–90°F — fire ants forage most actively in that range. In NC that means late afternoon or evening applications from about April through October. Midday applications in summer heat are much less effective because the bait can degrade before enough workers pick it up. And again — no rain in the 24 hours after application. If it rains shortly after you apply, you've wasted the product and need to reapply once things dry out.

Expect 7–14 days to see significant reduction in mound activity. If a colony is still clearly active at 3 weeks, follow up with the orange oil drench directly on that mound. Combining the two methods — bait for broad population suppression, drench for stubborn individual mounds — gets you faster and more complete results than either alone.
Is there anything I can do to make the beds less attractive to them in the first place?

Some things help, though I won't oversell it — raised beds hit almost every criterion fire ants look for: warm, loose, moist soil. You're working against the environment a bit.

The most practical preventive step is reducing moisture variation. Fire ants frequently move into garden beds during dry spells because the irrigated soil is one of the only reliably moist spots nearby. Switching from overhead watering to drip irrigation keeps the soil surface drier while still watering roots — that surface moisture gradient is part of what attracts nesting scouts. It won't eliminate the problem but makes your beds a less obvious target compared to the dry hardpan around them.

Keep the perimeter mowed and disturbed. Ants often establish satellite colonies in tall grass and weedy margins and then move inward. Regularly mowing, cultivating, or mulching that border disrupts staging areas. A 2-foot wide strip of regularly disturbed or heavily mulched ground around the bed edges does more than most people expect.

Diatomaceous earth applied as a physical barrier along the exterior edges of the beds has mixed evidence but some real-world support — it dehydrates insects that crawl through it. It won't stop a determined colony, but can slow scouting workers. You have to reapply after rain, which limits its practical value in NC's wet springs and summers.

Honestly, though, the biggest lever for long-term reduction is population pressure management across your whole yard — not just the beds. Two spinosad bait applications per year, spring and fall, working out about 15–20 feet beyond the garden perimeter, does more cumulative good than any physical barrier. You're reducing the regional colony density that's constantly probing your beds for new real estate.

What do I need for a basic indoor seed starting setup? I want to keep costs low.

You really only need four things: containers, a growing medium, light, and warmth. Here's where to spend money and where not to.

Containers: Exhaust free options before buying anything. Toilet paper rolls, plastic yogurt cups and deli containers with drainage holes punched in the bottom, or egg cartons all work for starting seeds. If you do buy, 72-cell plug trays run $3–4 each and are the most space-efficient option. Shallow is fine — you'll pot up before roots get cramped.

Growing medium: This is the one place not to cut corners. Don't use garden soil or regular potting mix — both compact and crust in small cells, which suffocates seedlings. A bag of seed starting mix (Pro-Mix, Jiffy, or a store brand) runs $10–15 and fills multiple trays. Alternatively, a 50/50 mix of vermiculite and perlite is cheap, drains excellently, and germination rates are great — just be aware it has no nutrients, so you'll need to start dilute liquid feeding once seedlings have their first true leaves.

Light: This is where most people go wrong without spending much money. A south-facing window almost never provides enough intensity for stocky seedlings during NC winter — you'll get leggy, weak plants. A basic 4-foot two-bulb T8 shop light from any hardware store costs $20–30 and works well hung 2–3 inches above the seedlings on an adjustable chain. Run it 14–16 hours a day. Cheap LED grow light strips in the $15–25 range on Amazon also work. Intensity and proximity matter far more than fancy full-spectrum labeling.

Warmth: Most vegetable seeds want 70–85°F soil to germinate well. The top of a refrigerator stays around 75°F and is a classic free heat source. A seedling heat mat costs $20–30 and is worth it specifically for peppers, tomatoes, and eggplant, which really want 80–85°F at the root zone. Once seeds sprout, they no longer need bottom heat — move them under the lights.

For NC timing: start peppers and eggplant indoors in late January to mid-February, tomatoes in mid-February to early March. Summer crops like squash, cucumbers, and melons direct-seed after your last frost — starting them indoors is usually more trouble than it's worth because they transplant poorly and catch up fast.

Total budget for a functional setup: $40–60, with the light being the main cost. Everything else can be improvised or found cheap.

What's the best cover crop mix for fixing nitrogen in NC?

For straight nitrogen fixation, you want legumes, and in NC the most practical window is fall-planted covers that overwinter and get terminated in spring before your main crops go in.

The workhorse mix for NC is crimson clover plus hairy vetch. Crimson clover (Trifolium incarnatum) is practically a state staple — you see it blooming along roadsides every April. Seed at 15–20 lbs per acre (roughly 0.35–0.45 lbs per 1,000 sq ft) from mid-September through October. Hairy vetch (Vicia villosa) is more winter-hardy, handles the mountains well, and is a heavier nitrogen fixer — up to 100–150 lbs N per acre at full maturity if it's properly inoculated. Seed at 20–30 lbs per acre (0.45–0.70 lbs per 1,000 sq ft). Mixed together, use about half the rate of each.

Austrian winter peas are another solid option, especially in Piedmont and mountain zones. Seed at 60–90 lbs per acre (1.4–2 lbs per 1,000 sq ft) from September through early October. Not as cold-hardy as hairy vetch but terminates easily in spring and breaks down quickly, which matters if you need to plant soon after.

One thing that makes or breaks legume covers: inoculation. The seeds need the right Rhizobium bacteria to actually form nitrogen-fixing nodules on their roots. In established soils that have grown legumes recently, native populations may be sufficient, but in new beds or depleted soils, don't assume. Inoculant packets cost $5–8 and treat several pounds of seed. Without it, legumes can still grow but pull nitrogen from soil like any other plant rather than fixing it from the air.

Termination timing: you capture maximum nitrogen when the cover is at full bloom — that's when biomass and N content peak. Mow or crimp at that point, or till it under. Wait at least 2–3 weeks before transplanting into terminated cover in warm weather; longer (4+ weeks) in cool spring conditions because decomposition slows significantly below 50°F.

One honest note: a single season of vetch or clover is a meaningful contribution — 50–120 lbs N per acre equivalent is typical — but it's not a miracle fix for depleted soil. If you're starting from a rough baseline, run a soil test through the NCDA&CS lab in Raleigh ($4 per sample) before assuming nitrogen is even your main limiting factor. Calcium, pH, and organic matter often matter more.

For summer fallow, cowpeas are the NC standby — seed after last frost at 80–100 lbs per acre and they'll fix nitrogen while smothering summer weeds at the same time.

Is there a way to manage Southern blight organically? I lost half my garden to it last summer.

Southern blight (Sclerotium rolfsii) is one of the toughest soilborne pathogens we deal with in NC — the combination of heat, humidity, and sandy or clay soils across most of the state creates a perfect environment for it. The good news is there are organic strategies that genuinely work, but you have to be systematic.

First, the biology you need to understand: S. rolfsii survives as sclerotia, which look like small mustard seeds scattered in the top 2-3 inches of soil. These structures can stay viable for years. The disease is most explosive above 85°F with wet conditions — classic NC July and August. When you saw that white mycelial mat at the soil line, the sclerotia were already spreading outward in a radius around it.

Here's what actually moves the needle organically:

Soil solarization is your most powerful tool. After your last spring harvest, cover the bed with clear 1-2 mil plastic sheeting for 4-6 weeks — mid-June through late July is ideal in NC. Soil temperatures at 2-4 inches can reach 130-140°F, which kills sclerotia. Research at NC State has documented 60-80% reduction in sclerotia viability after a good solarization. Clear plastic works better than black because it transmits solar radiation rather than just absorbing it.

Trichoderma-based biocontrols are your second line. Products containing Trichoderma harzianum — RootShield is the most commonly available OMRI-listed option — work by parasitizing sclerotia in the soil. Apply as a drench at the root zone before transplanting at about 1 oz per gallon of water, and reapply every 3-4 weeks during the growing season. It won't eliminate blight in heavily infested soil on its own, but it significantly reduces colonization when combined with other practices.

Remove infected plants immediately — don't compost them. The moment you see the white mat, pull the plant along with 2-3 inches of surrounding soil and bag it for the trash. Every day of delay is another 1-2 inches of outward spread.

Pull mulch back from plant stems. This is counterintuitive, but dense organic mulch right at the soil line creates ideal conditions for blight. During peak summer, keep mulch at least 6-8 inches away from stems of susceptible crops.

Deep tillage helps reduce pressure. Sclerotia can't germinate well from below 4-5 inches. If you till, incorporate and bury sclerotia to 6-8 inches. This doesn't eliminate them but reduces the population in the zone where they cause damage.

One thing worth knowing: Southern blight is significantly more aggressive in acidic soils. If your pH is below 6.0, liming to 6.5 reduces severity noticeably — not because lime kills the fungus, but because higher pH shifts the soil microbial community toward organisms that compete with it. Have you had a recent soil test done?
I haven't tested in a couple years. But more urgently — which crops should I avoid planting in those beds this season?

S. rolfsii has a host range of over 500 plant species, which is part of what makes it so frustrating. But susceptibility varies a lot, and you can plan around it.

Here's a practical ranking for NC vegetable gardens:

Most susceptible — avoid in your infested beds this season: tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, basil (extremely susceptible, almost always fatal), snap beans and lima beans, peanuts, squash, cucumbers, and okra. These are your high-risk crops and they'll likely get hit again under high inoculum pressure.

Moderate susceptibility: sweet potatoes, brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, kale, collards). They get it, but less aggressively and usually later in the season when they're already mature.

Lower susceptibility — good rotation choices: sweet corn is genuinely useful here, because grasses and grass-family crops are largely resistant. Planting corn for a season in a hot spot measurably reduces sclerotia populations. Garlic and onions are also excellent — alliums produce sulfur compounds with natural antifungal activity that suppresses multiple soil pathogens. Parsley, cilantro, dill, and most culinary herbs except basil are fine.

The practical move this season: dedicate your infested bed to sweet corn, garlic, or onions while you run solarization on it. Use your cleanest beds for tomatoes and peppers. Then rotate those crops into the treated bed next year after you've knocked the population down.

Before you do anything else, though — get that soil test submitted to the NCDA&CS lab. It's $4 and takes 2-3 weeks. If your pH is below 6.0, applying lime now (at a rate based on the test recommendation) costs almost nothing and will reduce your blight pressure meaningfully by midsummer. NC State Extension also has a plant disease fact sheet on S. rolfsii (Plant Disease Note 713) with photos to confirm you're actually dealing with blight and not Pythium or Rhizoctonia, which have similar symptoms but different management.

I'm a complete beginner. What's the most important thing to focus on in January in Fayetteville area?

Welcome — Fayetteville puts you in Zone 8a, which is a real advantage. You have a longer growing season than most of the country and you can grow a lot of things that gardeners farther north only dream about.

For a complete beginner, January's single most important job is getting a soil test submitted. I know that sounds less exciting than planting something, but the decisions you make this month set up everything else. Most soil in the Fayetteville area — Cumberland County sits on the Coastal Plain — tends to be sandy, acidic, and low in organic matter. If you plant into soil with a pH of 5.2 and depleted nutrients without knowing it, you'll spend the whole season wondering why your plants look sick. Lime takes 2-3 months to fully change soil pH, so if you apply it in January based on your results, it'll be working by the time spring planting season hits.

Here's how to get it done: go to the Cumberland County Cooperative Extension office at 301 East Mountain Drive. They'll give you a free sample bag and submission form. Take 6-8 small cores from different spots in your garden area, going 4-6 inches deep, mix them in a clean bucket, and put about 1 cup of the mixture in the bag. Mail or drop it off, pay the $4 fee, and you'll get results back in 2-3 weeks with specific lime and fertilizer recommendations tailored to vegetable gardening.

Beyond soil testing, the other high-value January task is planning what you want to grow and ordering seeds. Popular vegetable varieties sell out by February. For NC growing conditions, Southern Exposure Seed Exchange (based in Virginia, bred for the Southeast) and Sow True Seed out of Asheville are both excellent sources with varieties selected for our climate.

If you want an actual planting task this month: start short-day onion seeds indoors. Varieties like 'Yellow Granex,' 'Candy,' or 'Georgia Sweet' work well in this area. Sow them in a tray under a grow light now, and they'll be ready to transplant outside in late February or early March. Long-day onion varieties (most of what you see at big box stores) don't bulb properly in NC, so pay attention to that when ordering.

Don't feel overwhelmed. If you only do one thing in January, submit that soil test. Everything else can build on what you learn from it.
OK I want to do the soil test. Can I just buy one of those home test kits from the hardware store instead?

You can, but I'd steer you away from them for your situation. The home test kits — the ones with the color-chart capsules — give you a rough ballpark on pH and sometimes NPK, but they're not accurate enough to make good liming and fertilization decisions. You might find out your pH is 'acidic' but not know whether you need 5 lbs of lime per 100 sq ft or 20 lbs. That difference matters a lot.

The NC state lab test is genuinely better in every way except speed. Here's why it's worth the trip:

It tests actual nutrient levels at a lab, not a color reaction you're eyeballing. The results come with a specific recommendation — they'll tell you exactly how much lime to apply for the crop you're growing, and what fertilizer to add. It costs $4. Home test kits run $15-25 and give you less useful information.

The process at the Extension office takes about 10 minutes. The address is 301 East Mountain Drive, Fayetteville — it's in the Agriculture Building. They're open Monday through Friday during regular business hours. You can also download the submission form from ncagr.gov/agronomic/soiltest if you want to fill it out ahead of time and save a few minutes.

When you fill out the form, there's a section asking what you're growing. Write 'vegetable garden.' That's the code the lab uses to calibrate their recommendations specifically for food crops, which have different nutrient needs than lawns or shrubs.

One practical note: January is a great time to submit because the lab isn't backed up yet. By March they get slammed and turnaround can stretch to 3-4 weeks. Submit now and you'll have results in about 2 weeks, leaving plenty of time to apply lime before your spring planting window opens in late February.

What are the best companion plants for squash in NC?

The classic Three Sisters combination — corn, beans, and squash together — is as good as it gets and has hundreds of years of proof behind it in the Southeast. Corn gives beans something to climb, beans fix nitrogen at the root zone (roughly 50-100 lbs per acre over a season), and squash leaves create a dense ground cover that holds moisture and crowds out weeds. For best results, plant corn in a block at least 4 plants wide rather than a single row — it pollinates by wind and needs proximity to set ears well. Plant beans at the base of corn once it's 6 inches tall, and let squash sprawl outward from the edges.

Beyond the Three Sisters, here are companions specifically useful for NC conditions:

Nasturtiums planted around the perimeter of your squash patch act as a trap crop for aphids — the aphids colonize them preferentially and leave your squash alone. They also appear to deter squash bugs, which are one of the worst pests we deal with here. Bonus: the flowers and leaves are edible and make a decent peppery salad green.

It also has a long-standing reputation for repelling squash bugs — the evidence is mostly observational rather than rigorously studied, but experienced NC gardeners swear by it, and it costs nothing to try. This matters in NC because root-knot nematodes are widespread in our sandy Coastal Plain and Piedmont soils and they damage squash roots significantly. Radishes planted around squash are quick to mature and won't compete for long. Some growers report they confuse squash vine borers; the evidence is thin, but they're harvested in 25-30 days and the space is freed up anyway.

I got my soil test results back from NC State. Can you help me understand what they mean? My pH is 6.5, P-I is 100, K-I is 75, and organic matter is 3.5%.

Good news — your soil is in genuinely good shape. Here's what each number means in practical terms.

pH 6.5 is nearly ideal for a vegetable garden. The optimal range for most vegetables is 6.0-6.8. At 6.5, your macronutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) are all highly plant-available, and micronutrients like iron, manganese, and zinc are accessible too. You don't need lime or sulfur right now. If you ever want to grow blueberries, keep them in a separate area — they need pH 4.5-5.5 and can't share a bed that's been limed to 6.5.

P-I (Phosphorus Index) of 100 means your phosphorus level is High. NC State uses an index scale where 0-25 is Low, 26-50 is Medium, 51-100 is High, and above 100 is Very High. At 100 you're at the top of the High range. Do not add phosphorus fertilizer this year — there's nothing for plants to gain from more phosphorus when they already have plenty, and excess phosphorus runs off into waterways and contributes to algae problems in our rivers. This reading is common in beds that have received years of compost, since compost carries phosphorus even when it's primarily used for organic matter.

K-I (Potassium Index) of 75 is also in the High range. Same situation: you have adequate potassium and don't need to target it specifically. If you use a balanced granular fertilizer for nitrogen (more on that below), the small amount of potassium it contains is fine, but don't seek out high-potassium amendments like greensand or kelp meal this season.

Organic matter at 3.5% is excellent for North Carolina. The average NC soil runs 1-2% organic matter — our Coastal Plain and Piedmont soils are naturally sandy or heavily weathered and don't hold organic matter the way soils in cooler climates do. At 3.5%, you have strong water retention, active soil biology with good nutrient cycling, and good structure. Keep doing whatever you've been doing — regular compost additions, minimal tillage, maybe cover crops — and this number will stay healthy. It takes years to build and years to lose, so you're in a good position.

The main thing you'll still need to manage is nitrogen. Nitrogen doesn't show up in these index numbers because it doesn't stay put in soil the way P and K do — it cycles through constantly. A vegetable garden generally needs 2-3 lbs of actual nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft per season, applied in split doses during the growing season rather than all at once. If you add 2-3 inches of finished compost annually, that contributes roughly 0.5-0.75 lbs of slow-release nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft, so factor that in and supplement with a nitrogen source like blood meal (12-0-0), feather meal, or fish emulsion at transplanting and again at midseason.

Honestly, with numbers like these, your main job is maintenance. Don't over-fertilize chasing higher numbers — you're already where you need to be.

What should I fill my raised beds with? I've seen lots of conflicting advice.

The conflicting advice comes from a real tension between the theoretically ideal mix and what's practical to source and afford. Let me give you a straightforward answer that works well for NC conditions.

A 60/30/10 blend is a solid, proven starting point:

60% quality topsoil. Not bagged 'garden soil' from a big box store if you can help it — that product is inconsistent, often mostly peat, and compacts badly over time. Source bulk topsoil from a local landscape supply company. In most NC markets you'll pay $25-45 per cubic yard. Ask specifically for screened topsoil and ask where it came from. You want a loamy texture, not clay-heavy subsoil that someone screened and relabeled.

30% mature compost. This is the most important ingredient. It feeds soil biology, improves drainage if your topsoil leans clay, and improves water retention if it leans sandy — which describes most of NC. Blend from multiple sources when you can: yard waste compost plus mushroom compost plus aged manure gives you more diverse nutrients and biology than any single source. Many NC counties sell bulk compost made from yard waste at very reasonable prices through their solid waste programs.

10% perlite or coarse vermiculite. This keeps the mix from compacting as the organic matter breaks down over the years. It's a nice-to-have rather than essential — if budget is tight, skip it and just plan to top-dress with compost each season.

What to avoid: pure compost beds shrink 30-40% in the first year as the material breaks down — you'll have sunken gardens by fall. Bagged 'raised bed mix' from big box stores is often primarily peat moss, which is hydrophobic when it dries out and requires constant watering to rewet. Fill dirt or clay subsoil compacts into concrete and drowns roots.

For a standard 4x8 bed at 12 inches deep, you need about 32 cubic feet — roughly 1.2 cubic yards. Buying bulk is dramatically cheaper than bags. A cubic yard of topsoil costs $30-50; the same volume in bags would run $150 or more. If you're building multiple beds, call a landscape supplier and have it delivered.

One NC-specific note: whether you're in the Piedmont with red clay or the Coastal Plain with sandy, low-organic soil, raised beds let you sidestep your native soil situation entirely. The mix above will outperform almost any unamended NC in-ground soil from day one.
How deep should the beds be? I was going to do 6 inches.

Six inches will grow some things fine, but you'll hit limits faster than you'd expect and probably wish you'd gone deeper once you see how root systems develop.

Here's the practical breakdown by depth:

6 inches works for: lettuce, spinach, arugula, radishes, green onions, most culinary herbs like basil, parsley, and cilantro. If you're building a dedicated salad greens bed on a tight budget, 6 inches is acceptable.

8-10 inches covers most vegetables: beans, peppers, chard, kale, collards, brassicas, cucumbers, and summer squash. This is a reasonable minimum for a general-purpose bed.

12 inches is where I'd aim if you can do it. Tomatoes, eggplant, and zucchini put down significant root systems and will visibly outperform the same plants grown in a 6-inch bed — better drought tolerance, bigger yields, less wilting on hot afternoons. Twelve inches also gives you a buffer as the mix settles, because it will settle several inches in the first year as organic matter breaks down.

12-18 inches is necessary for root crops: carrots, parsnips, beets, and potatoes. Put carrots in a 6-inch bed and you'll get stubby, forked, frustrated roots. If you want to grow root crops, build at least one deeper bed specifically for them.

The cost argument for going deeper is actually pretty compelling. If you're already buying lumber and sourcing materials, the difference between 6 inches and 12 inches is roughly 0.6 cubic yards of additional mix per 4x8 bed — maybe $30-50 more in materials. You're building infrastructure that will last 10-15 years; that extra $40 pays off fast.

If cost is genuinely the limiting factor, there's a legitimate technique called hugelkultur: fill the bottom 4-6 inches with logs, wood scraps, cardboard, or straw, then put your soil mix on top. The wood acts as a slow-release sponge — it holds moisture during dry spells and breaks down over years, adding organic matter. It's not a workaround or a hack; it's a well-documented European technique that works fine in NC conditions. If you have wood debris around, it costs nothing.

What are you planning to grow? That'll tell me whether 6 inches actually meets your needs or whether it's worth going deeper.

I keep hearing about the 'soil food web.' Can you explain what that is and why it matters for my garden?

The soil food web is the community of organisms living in your soil and the feeding relationships connecting them. Think of it as a multi-story apartment building: bacteria and fungi on the ground floor breaking down organic matter, protozoa and nematodes on the next floor eating those bacteria and fungi, then predatory nematodes and microarthropods (mites, springtails) eating them, up through beetles, earthworms, and eventually birds and moles at the top.

Here's why it matters practically: nutrients don't just sit in the soil waiting for roots to grab them. They cycle through living bodies. When a protozoan eats a bacterium, it digests what it needs and excretes the excess nitrogen as ammonium — right in the root zone, right when nearby plants need it. That's called the microbial loop, and it's why biologically active soil can feed plants more efficiently than a bag of synthetic fertilizer, which tends to leach out quickly in NC's frequent rain events, especially in our sandier Coastal Plain soils.

Fungi deserve particular attention. Mycorrhizal fungi colonize root systems and extend their reach by 10 to 100 times through threadlike hyphae. They trade phosphorus — which they're expert at scavenging from tiny pore spaces — for carbohydrates from the plant. In the Piedmont's clay-heavy soils, phosphorus gets bound up by iron and aluminum and becomes chemically unavailable. Mycorrhizal networks help plants access it anyway. A soil test from the NCDA&CS lab might show adequate total phosphorus, but biological activity determines how much actually reaches your plants.

What destroys the web: repeated tilling (physically shreds fungal hyphae and disrupts bacterial colonies), high rates of synthetic nitrogen (triggers a bacterial boom-and-bust cycle), fungicides (obvious), and letting the soil dry out completely for extended periods.

What builds it: finished compost adds microbial diversity and feeds existing populations; mulch feeds surface decomposers and moderates moisture; reduced tillage lets fungal networks persist across seasons; cover crops feed the web during off-season. In practical terms, a 2- to 3-inch layer of wood chip mulch over your beds does more for soil biology over two or three years than almost anything else you can buy or do. The biology builds underneath it, and you'll see the difference in how your plants handle drought and pest pressure.

NC State's soils extension publications go deep on this if you want the full picture — look for resources through the Center for Environmental Farming Systems as well, which has done a lot of work on biological soil health specific to our region.

My neighbor sprays pesticides on everything. I want to go fully organic. Is that realistic?

Fully organic is realistic — and honestly it's where most experienced home gardeners in NC end up after a few seasons. The transition is the hard part, not the destination.

Here's the honest version: the first year or two can be rougher as your garden's pest-predator balance gets established. Your neighbor's sprays are almost certainly killing beneficial insects that would otherwise be working in your yard too, so you're starting behind. Give yourself two to three seasons before you judge the system.

The approach that actually works:

**Build healthy soil first.** Plants growing in biologically active, well-nourished soil are genuinely less susceptible to pest damage — this isn't feel-good talk, it's plant physiology. Stressed, nitrogen-imbalanced plants emit volatile compounds that attract pests. Get a soil test through NCDA&CS ($4 for a basic test) and fix what's off before you plant.

**Learn to identify what you're dealing with.** The vast majority of insects you'll see in your garden are neutral or beneficial. NC State Extension has an excellent insect identification resource online — use it before doing anything. Spraying something you can't identify is how beneficial insect populations get wiped out.

**Use physical controls proactively.** Floating row cover stops squash vine borers, cucumber beetles, and flea beetles before they're ever a problem. This is more reliable than any spray, organic or otherwise.

What are the best companion plants for cucumbers in NC?

Here are the companions that actually earn their place with cucumbers in NC:

**Nasturtiums** are probably the most useful. They act as aphid magnets in a productive way — drawing aphids off your cucumbers while simultaneously attracting the ladybugs and parasitic wasps that eat them. Plant 12 to 18 inches away from your cucumber row. Bonus: the flowers are edible and the leaves add a peppery bite to salads.

**Dill** attracts beneficial wasps that parasitize cucumber beetle larvae and eggs. Let it bolt and flower — that's when it does its job. Keep it at least 12 inches away and plant it after your cucumbers are established, not at the same time. Mature dill can inhibit cucumber germination if they're started together in close proximity.

**French marigolds** (Tagetes patula, the small ones — not African marigolds) are worth planting densely around the bed perimeter, 6-inch spacing. Root-knot nematodes are a serious problem in NC's sandy Coastal Plain and Piedmont soils, and French marigolds produce compounds that suppress nematode populations when planted thickly. Till them into the soil at season's end to maximize the effect.

**Bush beans** fix nitrogen, which cucumbers — as heavy feeders — will appreciate. Keep them 18 inches from your cucumber row so they're not competing for trellis space.

**Sunflowers** provide light afternoon shade during NC's brutal July and August heat, especially in zones 7b and 8a. Cucumbers will often climb the stalks voluntarily. Plant on the west or southwest side of your cucumber row.

**Avoid** planting cucumbers near sage or strongly aromatic herbs, and keep them well away from potatoes — they share disease pressure including several wilts.

One thing more important than any companion planting combination in NC: cucumber beetles. Both the spotted and striped varieties vector bacterial wilt, and once a plant is infected there's no saving it. Use floating row cover from transplant through first flowering, then remove it for pollination. That single practice will do more for your cucumber harvest than everything else combined.

We got 0.75 inches of rain this week. Do I still need to water my beans?

Probably, but it depends on your soil type and current temperatures. Beans generally want about 1 inch of water per week, so you're a quarter inch short on paper — but whether that matters right now depends on what the soil is actually holding.

In the Piedmont or mountains with clay-loam soil and highs in the 70s to low 80s, 0.75 inches might carry you fine for another three to four days. In the Coastal Plain with sandy soil, or anywhere if temperatures are pushing into the 90s, that rain may have already largely drained through or evaporated.

Best check: push your finger 2 inches into the soil at the root zone. If it's dry at that depth, water. If it's still damp, wait and check again tomorrow.

One stage-specific note: if your beans are actively flowering or filling pods, don't let them stress at all. That's the window when water deficit causes the most yield loss — flowers drop and pods stay small. Consistent moisture during pod set is critical.
It's been really hot this week, mid-90s. And the soil here is pretty sandy — I'm near the coast.

Water them today. In sandy coastal soil at 95°F, that 0.75 inches is essentially gone by now.

Here's the math: sandy soil holds roughly 0.75 to 1 inch of available water per foot of depth, compared to 1.5 to 2 inches for a good loam. On top of that, evapotranspiration in mid-90s heat in eastern NC can pull 0.2 to 0.3 inches per day out of the root zone. Do the math across a week and there's nothing left for your beans to draw on.

Give them a thorough soak — aim for 1 inch of water applied, which works out to roughly 0.6 gallons per square foot of bed. Drip irrigation or a soaker hose is the right tool in that heat; overhead watering loses 20 to 30 percent to evaporation before it even hits the soil, and wet foliage in warm weather invites fungal problems on beans.

Water in the early morning if you can. You lose less to evaporation, and leaves dry off quickly, which keeps disease pressure down.

For the rest of the season: with sandy coastal soil in summer, plan on watering every two to three days rather than once a week. You can use slightly less water per session since the soil drains fast, but it can't hold a full week's reserve the way heavier soils can. And if you haven't already, a 2-inch layer of straw mulch around your bean plants will cut evapotranspiration loss noticeably — it's one of the single best things you can do for sandy soil in an eastern NC summer.

How do I save seeds from my beans? I want to start being more self-sufficient.

Beans are the perfect starting point for seed saving — they're self-pollinating, so they close and fertilize themselves before the flower even fully opens. That means variety integrity is easy to maintain and the process is forgiving.

**Step 1: Designate seed plants early.**
Mid-season, pick your strongest, most productive plants and mark them with a stake. Don't harvest any beans from these plants for eating — let every pod go to full maturity. Saving seed from your best performers rather than just any random plant is how you gradually adapt a variety to your specific soil and microclimate over years. That's how landrace varieties develop.

**Step 2: Leave pods on the vine until fully dry.**
You want pods that have turned papery, tan or brown, and crinkly. The seeds inside should be rock-hard with no give when you press them. This usually happens 60 to 70 days past normal snap-bean harvest stage — so plan for it when you're deciding which plants to dedicate.

**Step 3: Watch the weather.**
Harvest before NC's fall rains move in. Wet conditions at this stage cause mold and can trigger premature sprouting inside the pod. If rain is coming and your pods aren't fully dry yet, pull the whole plant and hang it upside down in a dry, ventilated space — a garage or shed works well. Give pulled plants another two to three weeks of hang-drying before shelling.

**Step 4: Shell and do a final dry.**
Shell the pods and spread seeds in a single layer on a screen or paper plate for one to two weeks at room temperature indoors. This step is critical in NC's humidity. Beans can feel dry to the touch but still hold 12 to 15 percent moisture content, which causes rot or lost germination in storage. Target is below 8 percent moisture. A simple check: put your seeds in a jar with a tablespoon of dry white rice and seal it. If the rice clumps after a week, your seeds still need more drying time.

**Step 5: Storage.**
Once thoroughly dry, store seeds in an airtight glass jar with a silica gel packet in a cool, dark location. A consistent 40 to 50°F is ideal — a spare refrigerator shelf works well. Properly stored beans hold viable germination for three to four years, sometimes longer. Label everything with variety name and harvest year; memory is unreliable after two seasons.

**On variety purity:**
Since beans self-pollinate, cross-pollination rates are low — around 1 to 2 percent. For home purposes, you can grow two varieties with as little as 25 feet of separation and maintain reasonable purity. If you're growing just one variety, no worries at all.

NC State Extension publication AG-608 covers seed saving for common vegetables in more depth if you want a good reference to keep on hand.

What's the difference between the free NC State soil test and the ones you pay for?

Good question to start with — the free test is genuinely useful and most home gardeners never need anything more than it.

First, a small clarification: the free test comes from the NCDA&CS Agronomic Division (a state lab that works closely with NC State Extension, but technically a separate agency). It's free from April 1 through November 30; from December through March there's a $4/sample fee. What you get: pH, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, manganese, copper, and lime and fertilizer recommendations written specifically for whatever crop you tell them you're growing. That's a solid panel for diagnosing most common problems and making the right amendments.

What it doesn't give you: organic matter percentage, cation exchange capacity (CEC), base saturation ratios, or nitrate-N. It also won't run a full sodium analysis or give you the kind of mineral balance data that some soil health advocates want.

The paid private labs — A&L Eastern Laboratories (common in the Southeast), Logan Labs, and Ward Labs are the ones most serious NC gardeners use — typically run $20–35 for a comprehensive test. You'll get organic matter %, CEC, and base saturation percentages for calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium, and hydrogen. Some gardeners want those numbers to dial in soil biology and mineral balance rather than just chasing NPK targets.

For a typical vegetable bed or lawn situation, the free NCDA&CS test tells you everything you need to act on. The private labs earn their cost when you're trying to understand why a soil that looks fine on paper isn't performing, or when you're managing a no-till or cover-crop-heavy system and want to track organic matter gains over multiple years.
Is the free test really good enough for vegetables? I've heard it doesn't test organic matter.

For most vegetable gardening purposes, yes — it gives you what you need to take meaningful action. The absence of an OM reading is less of a gap than it sounds, because the recommendation for almost every NC vegetable bed with subpar soil is the same regardless: add 2–4 inches of finished compost worked into the top 6–8 inches, every year. You don't need a lab number to arrive at that conclusion.

Where an OM percentage from a private lab becomes genuinely useful is when you're tracking measurable improvement over years in a no-till or heavily amended system. Watching that number climb from 1.8% to 3.5% over four seasons is satisfying and confirms your practices are working — but it's not required to make good decisions along the way.

The free test's real strength is the lime recommendation. Getting pH right — most NC vegetable crops want 6.0–6.5, and our native soils tend to run acidic, often in the 5.0–5.8 range — is probably the single highest-leverage thing you can do for a vegetable garden. The NCDA&CS lab calculates exactly how much lime your specific soil texture needs to buffer to your target pH. Private labs give you a pH reading but often provide more generic lime guidance.

One thing worth knowing: you can add on individual enhanced tests through NCDA&CS — including organic matter — for a small additional fee per sample. Check the current menu on the NCDA&CS Agronomic Division website before you submit. It changes occasionally but it's usually a few dollars per add-on.

Bottom line: submit the free test, follow the lime recommendation to the letter, apply compost generously, and you'll be making better decisions than the majority of home vegetable gardeners in the state.
Okay, how do I actually collect and submit a sample?

Straightforward process once you know the steps.

**Collecting the sample:**
Use a clean trowel or soil probe — no galvanized metal, which can contaminate zinc and copper readings. Take 8–12 sub-samples from random spots across the area you're testing, zigzagging through the bed rather than sampling in a line or just one corner. For a vegetable garden, go 6 inches deep; for a lawn, 4 inches is standard. Combine all sub-samples in a clean plastic bucket, mix thoroughly, then scoop out about 1 cup of that blended mix as your actual sample. This compositing step averages out the natural variability within a bed and gives you a representative reading.

Keep distinct areas as separate samples: your vegetable garden, your lawn, and an ornamental bed are three different ecosystems with different management histories and should be tested separately.

**Submitting:**
Pick up soil boxes and submission forms free at your county Cooperative Extension office — every county in NC has one, and many also have them at local feed and seed stores. Fill the box to the fill line (don't pack it, just fill), complete the form including what crop you're growing and what amendments you've applied recently (this affects their recommendations), and drop it off at the Extension office. They batch-ship samples to the Agronomic Division lab in Raleigh.

Results typically come back in 1–2 weeks during the off-season, 3–4 weeks during the spring rush in March and April when they're swamped. They'll come by email if you provide an address on the form, which is faster.

**Timing tip:** Sample in fall after your harvest wraps up if you can manage it. That gives you the whole winter to source lime, and lime takes 2–3 months to fully react and adjust soil pH — so fall application means your beds are dialed in by planting time in spring. Spring sampling works but you're often playing catch-up.

How do I terminate a cover crop without tilling?

The right method depends heavily on which cover crop you're terminating — they vary a lot in how easy they are to kill without tillage.

**Cereal rye (the most common NC winter cover):**
The gold standard no-till termination is crimping or rolling. You flatten the standing crop with a roller-crimper when it reaches anthesis — when you can actually see pollen shedding from the seed heads, typically late April in the NC Piedmont. At that growth stage the hollow stems crimp-to-kill reliably, and the allelopathic compounds in the residue are at their peak, which suppresses weed germination for weeks afterward. A water-filled PVC roller-crimper is something many market gardeners build themselves for under $100. Timing is critical: crimp too early and the plants spring back up.

For smaller gardens without a roller, mow flat and then cover with a silage tarp — either black woven poly or impermeable black polyethylene — for 4–6 weeks. The combination of darkness, residue breakdown, and heat does the work. Tarping alone without mowing first also works but takes longer, sometimes 6–8 weeks in cool spring weather.

**Crimson clover, hairy vetch, Austrian winter peas (legumes):**
Easier to kill. Mow or crimp at early to full bloom. They're not as allelopathic as rye, so they decompose faster and provide a nitrogen flush to the soil (hairy vetch fixes 80–120 lbs N/acre in good stands). Mowing to 2–3 inches and leaving the residue as mulch is sufficient — these won't re-root the way rye can if conditions stay moist.

**Brassica cover crops — tillage radishes, turnips, mustard:**
Daikon-type radishes typically winter-kill on their own in NC zones 6b–7a, leaving behind decomposed channels in the soil. Mustard can be persistent; mow it at flowering before seed set. Mustard also has some biofumigant properties when incorporated, but that requires incorporation to be effective.

**General rules for all no-till termination:**
- Terminate at least 3–4 weeks before direct seeding into that bed. Fresh decomposing residue, especially from legumes and rye, can release compounds that suppress seed germination — the same allelopathy that suppresses weeds will hit your crops too if you're too hasty.
- For transplanting into standing rye (the classic no-till plasticulture method), you can do it right at crimping — transplants punch through the mulch layer and the thick residue suppresses weeds all season.
- Never let a cover crop reach full seed maturity before termination. Rye or clover volunteers from shattered seed will haunt you for years.

NC State Extension has a cover crop termination guide specific to our region with timing windows by crop and hardiness zone — it's worth bookmarking before you plant your covers each fall.

How do I plan succession plantings within a square foot garden framework?

The core idea is treating each square foot as an independent planting unit with its own timeline, and replanting it the moment — or slightly before — it's harvested. In North Carolina, where we have two productive growing seasons bookended by a brutal summer, this works really well, but it requires planning around the calendar rather than thinking in vague seasonal terms.

**The basic method:**
Once you know a crop's days-to-maturity (DTM), count backward from your target harvest date or forward from your sow date and record it on a grid chart. When that square is due to open up, you should already have transplants started or seeds staged to go in immediately. A simple 4x4 grid on paper or a spreadsheet works fine — some people use sticky notes flagged in the bed itself.

**In NC, plan around three planting windows:**

1. **Early spring (February–mid-April in the Piedmont, zone 7b):** Cool-season crops — lettuce, spinach, beets, carrots, radishes, peas, chard, kale, scallions. DTMs range from 25–35 days for radishes and salad mix up to 70–75 days for carrots and beets. Stagger plantings of fast crops every 2–3 weeks.

2. **Summer (June–July):** Most cool-season crops bolt or collapse in NC summer heat. Succession-plant heat-tolerant crops here: basil, beans (every 2 weeks gives continuous harvest), cucumbers, okra, and 'Fordhook Giant' chard (more heat-tolerant than colorful varieties). Or sow buckwheat in dormant squares — it flowers in 30 days, smothers weeds, attracts beneficials, and can be cut down before seed set to prepare the bed for fall.

3. **Fall (late July–October):** The best succession window in NC, hands down. Start staggering plantings of kale, collards, spinach, lettuce, Asian greens, arugula, beets, and turnips every 2–3 weeks beginning around August 1. In the Piedmont (Raleigh, Greensboro, Charlotte), your average first frost falls around October 15–22, so the math on your last sowing date matters. Spinach at 40 days DTM sown October 1 can still harvest before a hard freeze; lettuce sown October 15 might need a row cover assist.

**Practical management tips:**
- Log planting dates. Memory is unreliable when you have 16 squares going at different stages. A dated photo of the grid monthly takes 10 seconds.
- When a square finishes, work in a small amendment before replanting — about a quarter cup of compost per square foot. Rapid succession cropping depletes nutrients faster than a single long planting would.
- For crops that occupy a square for a full season (one tomato, one eggplant), you can't succession them in the same square, but you can start a second plant in a separate square 3–4 weeks after the first to extend your harvest window across the whole bed.
- Fast-turnover crops are your succession engines: radishes (25–30 days), cut-and-come-again salad mix (28–35 days), arugula (40 days). Build rotations around these.

**The NC-specific reality:**
Don't try to force continuous successions through July and August the way you would in the Pacific Northwest or the Upper Midwest. Heat and humidity will defeat you. Use midsummer as a reset and refuel period — mulch down dormant squares, grow buckwheat, let the soil breathe. Come early August, pivot hard into the fall succession push, which is honestly the most productive stretch of the NC garden year: cooling temps, fewer pests, and sugars concentrating in greens and roots in ways spring can't match.

I'm an experienced gardener. What's the most important thing to focus on in September in Greensboro/Triad Piedmont?

September in Greensboro is a race against the calendar, and the single most important focus is getting fall brassicas and root crops in the ground in the first two weeks of the month. If they're not in by September 15, you're giving up meaningful yield.

Here's the arithmetic: Greensboro's average first frost lands around October 19–22. Broccoli transplanted September 10 at 55 days DTM reaches harvest around November 4 — tight but solid, and a light frost actually improves flavor. Direct-sown 'Napoli' or 'Scarlet Nantes' carrots at 65–70 days need to be in the ground by September 1 to make it. Push those dates past mid-September and you're gambling on an extended fall, which happens — but you shouldn't plan on it.

**What to be doing right now:**
- Get broccoli, cabbage, and cauliflower transplants in the ground. Water them in with dilute fish emulsion at 1 tablespoon per gallon — September transplants need to establish roots fast in still-warm soil before growth slows. Set transplants at true depth; broccoli especially benefits from being set slightly deeper than it grew in the cell pack.
- Direct-sow spinach ('Bloomsdale Long Standing' or 'Tyee'), lettuce (any looseleaf type), Asian greens (tatsoi, mizuna, komatsuna), arugula, and hakurei turnips. These germinate readily in warm September soil and will be in full production by mid-October.
- Get a final sowing of beets in — 'Detroit Dark Red' or 'Chioggia' at 55–60 days can finish under row cover if frost comes early.
- Plant strawberry crowns or plug plants now. September 15–October 10 is the optimal establishment window for June-bearing varieties in the Piedmont. Plugs from NC-based nurseries establish faster than bare-root crowns ordered from out of state.

**Things that don't seem urgent but actually are:**
- Order your garlic now. You won't plant until October 1–15, but Porcelain hardnecks that do well here — 'Music,' 'Georgian Crystal,' 'Romanian Red' — sell out at reputable suppliers by late September. Get your order in.
- Cover crop any bed that won't be planted in the next 3 weeks. Cereal rye can be seeded through October 15 in your area; a rye/crimson clover mix at 2 lbs rye + 1 lb clover per 1,000 sq ft gives you weed suppression plus nitrogen fixation. Don't let bare soil sit.
- Pull summer crops the moment they decline. Every day a spent or diseased tomato or squash plant occupies a bed is a day something productive isn't growing there. Don't be sentimental about it.

**The bigger picture:**
Experienced Piedmont gardeners know the fall garden often out-produces spring if you stay aggressive through September. Pest pressure drops sharply, disease pressure eases as humidity falls, and the cooling temperatures concentrate sugars in greens and roots in ways our humid spring rarely allows. 'Winterbor' kale and collards that tasted mediocre in June will be genuinely good after the first frost in November. Don't let the lingering heat of early September fool you into waiting — the soil is still above 65°F, which is ideal for germination, and that window is closing.

Root-knot nematodes showed up in my soil test. How do I deal with this without fumigating?

Root-knot nematodes — mostly Meloidogyne incognita and M. arenaria in NC — are one of the nastier problems in our state's sandy soils, but there are genuinely effective non-fumigation approaches. The honest caveat: there's no single silver bullet, and you'll need a multi-pronged strategy applied over multiple seasons to get populations down to manageable levels.

**Soil solarization — your highest-impact single intervention:**
Clear polyethylene plastic (1.5–2 mil, not black — you need solar gain, not just heat retention) laid over moist, freshly worked soil in July and August generates lethal temperatures in the top 6–8 inches. You're aiming for 125°F+ at 2-inch depth, which NC summers can hit reliably in 4–6 weeks of full sun. Leave it down 6–8 weeks. This kills nematodes through the primary feeding zone — the top 8 inches — plus a meaningful reduction in soilborne fungal pathogens and weed seeds as a bonus. You'll knock back some beneficial organisms too, but they recolonize faster than root-knot nematodes do. Not compatible with no-till principles, but absolutely worth a one-time reset on a badly infested bed.

**Sunn hemp (Crotalaria juncea) — the cover crop NC State recommends most strongly:**
This is a tropical summer legume — plant after soil temps hit 65°F (mid-May in the Piedmont) at about 0.5–1 lb seed per 1,000 sq ft. It fixes nitrogen and produces compounds — primarily monocrotaline and related pyrrolizidine alkaloids — that are toxic to nematode juveniles. Grown as a solid stand for 60 days and terminated before seed set, sunn hemp consistently reduces root-knot nematode populations 60–80% in NC field trials. Incorporate it and wait 3 weeks before planting into that bed (it's allelopathic when fresh). This is your best summer-bed strategy if solarization isn't feasible.

**French marigolds as a trap/biofumigant crop:**
Tagetes patula specifically, not African marigolds (T. erecta), which have far less nematicidal activity. The varieties with documented suppression are 'Tangerine,' 'Single Gold,' and 'Petite Harmony.' They lure juvenile nematodes into root tissue, where alpha-terthienyl and bithienyl compounds kill them. The catch: you need dense solid plantings at 6-inch spacing covering the entire bed, maintained for 60–90 continuous days, then the whole stand incorporated. A few marigolds scattered around tomatoes accomplishes almost nothing. As a dedicated seasonal cover, they're legitimately effective.

**Chitin amendments — long-game soil biology:**
Crab or shrimp meal worked into the top 4 inches at 1–2 lbs per 100 sq ft feeds chitin-degrading soil bacteria — Streptomyces, Bacillus, and especially Pasteuria penetrans, which is an obligate parasite of Meloidogyne. These organisms also parasitize nematode eggs directly. This isn't a quick fix; it builds suppressive soil biology over multiple seasons. High-organic-matter soils (above 3% OM) are broadly less hospitable to nematode population explosions, so any practice that builds OM — compost, cover crops, reduced tillage — is pulling in the right direction.

**Resistant varieties — use these regardless of other strategies:**
Look for 'N' in the VFN designation on tomato tags. 'Celebrity,' 'Big Beef,' 'Amelia,' 'Mountain Magic,' and 'Plum Regal' all carry resistance. 'Beauregard' and 'Covington' sweet potatoes (both developed at NC State, widely adapted here) have solid tolerance. This doesn't eliminate nematodes, but resistance can allow productive harvests even in infested soil while other interventions are working.

**Poor-host rotation:**
Corn, small grains, most grasses, alliums (garlic, onions, leeks), and most brassicas are poor or non-hosts for M. incognita and won't feed the population. Rotating these into infested beds consistently is one of the simplest tools available. Conversely, avoid planting susceptible crops — tomatoes, peppers, squash, melons, sweet potatoes — in infested beds until you've worked the population down.

**A practical multi-season framework:**
- Year 1: Solarize in summer + plant brassicas or alliums in fall and spring.
- Year 2: Grow sunn hemp or French marigolds for the full summer season, then transplant resistant-variety tomatoes or peppers the following spring with chitin amendments incorporated.
- Year 3: Reassess. Full susceptible-variety plantings in beds with built-up OM and suppressive biology.

**One last thing:** nematodes travel in water flow and on soil-contaminated tools and equipment. If your infestation is localized to certain beds, clean tools between beds and be careful about introducing outside soil, fill, or transplants. That's how they spread.

How deep do raised beds need to be for tomatoes?

For tomatoes, aim for at least 12 inches of soil depth — that's the functional minimum. Eighteen inches is where they really perform well, giving the root system room to spread before it hits whatever's below.

Tomato roots can technically go 3-4 feet deep in loose soil, but the majority of feeder roots stay in the top 12-18 inches. That's where nutrient uptake and water absorption actually happen.

Here's the NC-specific good news: if your raised bed is sitting on native ground rather than concrete or pavers, the roots will eventually punch down into whatever's underneath. Even our heavy Piedmont clay holds moisture and nutrients reasonably well once established roots reach it. So a 12-inch bed over reasonably workable native soil is genuinely adequate for most seasons. If you're building over hardpan, compacted fill, or an impermeable surface, go 18 inches minimum.

One thing people overlook: bed width matters almost as much as depth. A tomato in a 12-inch-wide raised bed will be root-bound and dry out constantly. You want at least 24 inches of width per row of plants, and 36-48 inches is better for indeterminate varieties like Cherokee Purple or most heirlooms.

Also — don't line the bottom of the bed with landscape fabric. Let roots penetrate down. That clay subsoil acts as a slow-release moisture reservoir during our July and August dry spells.

Is it worth building a greenhouse in Charlotte area Piedmont? What could I do with it?

Yes, absolutely worth it — and Charlotte's zone 7b/8a climate is actually one of the better spots in NC to get value from a greenhouse because your winters are mild enough that a small heater handles most cold nights without huge fuel bills.

Here's what you can realistically do with a greenhouse in the Charlotte Piedmont:

**Year-round food production**: Lettuce, spinach, arugula, Asian greens, and most herbs grow happily through winter in an unheated greenhouse here. You're not fighting 10°F nights like the mountains — most of your winter is in the 30s and 40s overnight, which is fine for cold-hardy crops with just the passive heat gain from the structure.

**Earlier transplant starts**: Tomatoes and peppers started in January under glass can be ready to transplant by late March or early April — 6-8 weeks ahead of what you'd do starting seeds on a windowsill. That's a meaningful head start on your main-season crops.

**Overwintering tender perennials**: Potted fig trees, rosemary, citrus, lemon verbena, and similar marginally-hardy plants can live in the greenhouse November through March instead of dying back or getting killed in a hard freeze. Rosemary in particular is borderline in the Piedmont during severe winters — a greenhouse solves that permanently.

**Fall extension for heat lovers**: You can keep cucumbers, peppers, and basil producing well into November, which normally shuts down after first frost (typically late October in Charlotte).

**Propagation**: Cuttings from dahlias, salvias, figs, and other plants you want to multiply over winter.

The only real downside is summer heat management — a Charlotte greenhouse in July is brutal without good ventilation. Plan for that from day one and it's not a problem.
What size and style would you recommend? Should I buy a kit or build from scratch?

For most home gardeners in the Charlotte area, 8x12 or 10x12 feet is the sweet spot. Big enough to be genuinely productive, small enough to heat economically on cold nights. Smaller than that and you'll outgrow it in one season; jump to 12x20 and heating costs climb noticeably.

**Kit vs. build from scratch:**

*Polycarbonate panel kits* ($800–$2,500 — Palram, Rion, Juliana): This is where I'd point most people starting out. The 8mm or 10mm twin-wall polycarbonate holds heat dramatically better than glass or single-layer poly film — the trapped air between layers acts as insulation. Good kits assemble in a weekend with basic tools. Look specifically for kits rated for Southern wind loads and the occasional wet snow we get in the Piedmont.

*DIY hoop house* ($200–$600): EMT conduit or cattle panel hoops covered in 6-mil greenhouse poly film. Perfectly functional, and it lets you experiment cheaply before committing to a permanent structure. Downside: the poly film degrades in UV after 3-4 years and needs replacing, and it doesn't insulate as well as twin-wall polycarbonate.

*Timber frame custom build*: Beautiful and permanent, but realistically $4,000+ in materials unless you have the skills and salvaged materials.

**Orientation matters a lot in Charlotte**: Run the ridge east-west and put the long face south. Our winter sun angle at solstice is around 30–32°, so a south-facing wall catches dramatically more light than any other orientation. If you're on a sloped lot, account for that too — shade from a treeline to the south will cut your winter productivity significantly.

**The one thing most beginners undersize**: ventilation. A Charlotte greenhouse in April with the doors closed can hit 110–120°F by noon. Whatever kit you buy, make sure it has at least two roof vents — preferably with automatic vent openers (around $30–40 each) so you don't have to babysit it on warm spring days. This is not optional if you want healthy plants.

What's the most cost-effective irrigation setup for a complete beginner with 10x10 in-ground plot?

A soaker hose on a mechanical timer. Total cost: $35–55, and with basic care it'll last 5–7 years.

**What to buy:**
- 25–50 feet of flat soaker hose: $15–25 (Swan and Dramm both hold up well; avoid no-name brands that crack after one season)
- A mechanical twist-dial timer: $15–20 (the simple single-dial type, no batteries or programming — just set it and turn the knob)
- A Y-splitter for your spigot if you want to keep a regular hose available: $5–8

**Layout**: Zigzag the soaker hose across your 10x10 bed in parallel rows spaced about 12–18 inches apart. Connect it to the timer at the spigot. You're done.

**How long to run it in NC**: During peak summer (July–August), run it 25–35 minutes every morning. Spring and fall, every other morning is usually enough. The target is 1–1.5 inches of water per week total from irrigation plus rainfall. A simple way to calibrate: set a tuna can in the bed and see how much accumulates during a cycle.

**Why soaker hose beats overhead sprinklers for NC vegetable beds**: Water goes directly to the root zone, not the foliage. In our humid summers — July in the Piedmont routinely runs 70–80% relative humidity — wet foliage is a standing invitation to early blight, septoria leaf spot, and powdery mildew.
